messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Aleksander Nowak is a 28-year-old Polish-American man who works as a social media manager for a mid-sized marketing agency in Chicago. He lives with his long-term partner in a north-side apartment and, to most colleagues who interact with him through scheduled Slack messages and polished content calendars, presents as organised and dependable. He came to his first intake session speaking carefully, in sentences that felt rehearsed — because they were. Before any conversation of consequence, Aleksander runs through likely exchanges in his head, testing words for safety before he commits to them aloud.

He served two tours with a National Guard infantry unit and was medically separated at twenty-six following an incident during his second deployment in which the vehicle he was riding in was struck by an IED on a narrow road outside a forward operating base. The explosion killed one soldier seated beside him and left a second with catastrophic leg injuries. Aleksander was thrown clear of the vehicle but largely uninjured. What he remembers of the minutes that followed does not arrive as a coherent scene. There are pieces: the smell of burning, a hand — he cannot say whose — the sound of a rotary aircraft arriving overhead. The pieces do not connect into a story he can hold. Sometimes the grief and terror of that roadside come over him with full force while he is doing something entirely ordinary, and there is no image attached, no clear memory to point to — only the feeling, arriving without warning like a pressure change in the air. He has said more than once that when he tries to think about what happened, it feels less like remembering something he lived through and more like reading about a stranger's worst day. He had come to believe, quietly and with some shame, that a different man would have been in a different seat, would have reacted faster, would not have walked away while others did not.

In the two years since his separation, a set of habits formed that now shape his daily life in ways that have become difficult to ignore. He drives only when he is alone. Sitting in a passenger seat, or with anyone beside him, produces a physical reaction he cannot override — his chest tightens, his hands press flat against his thighs, and he watches the road with an attention that exhausts him. His partner has largely stopped asking to be driven anywhere, and the two of them have settled into an unspoken arrangement around this that neither has named directly. At his desk, he manages accounts that occasionally require sourcing or moderating news content, and on more than one occasion he has encountered images of injured people in user-generated posts — visible wounds, bloodied limbs — and found himself unable to continue working for the remainder of the afternoon, his body responding as though the image were something happening nearby rather than something on a screen. He routes his content review through filters where possible, and his supervisor believes this is a workflow preference.

Helicopter sounds, common enough over a city, reach him before he consciously registers them. By the time he identifies the source, his pulse is already elevated and he is scanning the room. He sleeps poorly, lying awake with a vigilance that feels necessary to him — he is certain, in those hours, that relaxing his attention would be a mistake. He startles badly when touched without warning, and his partner has learned to announce themselves before entering a room where Aleksander cannot see the door. He avoids anything that places his body under physical stress — he stopped running, avoids crowded transit, and declined an invitation to a gym class a colleague organised. He does not go near anything that resembles a uniform or a weapon, including a police officer standing outside a coffee shop he used to visit regularly.

What finally brought him to seek help was not a single event but an accumulation: his partner said, gently but directly, that they felt they were living with someone who was always waiting for something terrible to happen. Aleksander could not disagree. What he fears most, sitting in the intake chair, is that they are right — that this is simply who he is now, and that the person who existed before that road outside the FOB is not coming back.
